items.doc: David N. Baker SI-NEA oral history (2)
items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: By this time we were also going over to the Hampton's house to practice. They had a family band... That was me and David Young and the guys.

ctx.x: All the clubs along Indiana Avenue [also known as "The Avenue"]. There must have been probably 20 clubs. Each of them had a jam session night. You would go – some of them had the same night. We would go from one club to another, playing our blues and then leave and go to the next club and play blues. We had no more business than the man in the moon, most of the time, playing these clubs, because you had people like Pookie [Alonzo] Johnson; and Jimmy Coe; and Wes,
Buddy, and Monk Montgomery. These guys were the pros. The youngsters were me and Slide Hampton and guys like us.

items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dave and I were very close, because he was born one year before me, and we both played trombone. So we were very close. We were practicing together a lot.

ctx.x: Yeah, Middletown, Ohio. We lived there only for a short time. Then for some reason Indianapolis was very attractive for us, because there was a lot of music going on there, because there was an agent, a booking agent, that brought the bands to Indianapolis. They all came to Indianapolis to get their contracts before they went on their tours in the South, all the black bands. So we found that a place that was a very good musical environment to grow in. Right along – actually, I was raised with David Baker and…

items.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: David Baker was there and of course J.J. Johnson, we all started to learn to arrange right with learning to play the instrument.

ctx.x: I see. When did you first get the urge to become an arranger?

Well you know somebody was just asking me that question, and in the case of us, which are all the guys in Indianapolis, David Baker was there and of course J.J. Johnson, we all started to learn to arrange right with learning to play the instrument. Because we thought in order to be a complete musician you had to learn about theory, you had to learn about orchestration, you had to learn about arrangements, you had to learn about playing in the ensemble. So this was all a part of becoming a musician for us. And so…
I see. So it wasn’t really just like this separate decision, I can play now and then I need to be a writer too. Kind of just hand in hand? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
